statement: In adults treated in emergency departments for cannabis hyperemesis syndrome (repeated bouts of vomiting with regular heavy cannabis use), the evidence is insufficient to say whether capsaicin cream rubbed on the belly helps, as described in a 2024 systematic review of five studies with 386 patients (Sabbineni et al., 2024; AMSTAR 2 critically low). In the one small randomized trial (about 30 patients), nausea 30 minutes after the cream did not differ from a placebo cream, though more people had complete relief (29% against none) and nausea was lower at 60 minutes; of four non-randomized studies, one found fewer extra medicines and faster discharge (55% against 21% needing at most one more drug), one fewer extra medicines without a shorter stay, one no change in pain, and one no difference in stay or returns, with more hospital admissions after capsaicin (8 against 1, not significant). No serious side effects were reported, but the studies were small, mostly retrospective and at moderate to high risk of bias. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Cannabis hyperemesis syndrome means bouts of being sick again and again in some people who use a lot of cannabis for a long time. In hospital emergency rooms, some doctors rub a hot-pepper cream (capsaicin) on the belly. In one small fair test, it did not ease sickness more than a dummy cream after half an hour, though a few more people felt fully better. Other studies disagreed, so it is not known whether the cream helps.
population: Adults (some studies from age 16) treated for cannabis hyperemesis syndrome in North American emergency departments
exposure: Topical capsaicin cream applied in the emergency department (strengths are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: Placebo cream (one trial), patients not given capsaicin, the same patients' earlier visits, or symptoms before the cream
outcome: Nausea and pain scores, need for rescue medicines, time in the department, admissions, return visits
magnitude: Randomized trial: nausea at 30 min difference -2.0 cm (interval printed 0.2 to -4.2), not significant; complete resolution 29.4% against 0%. Non-randomized: 55% against 21% needing at most one more drug and 3.72 against 6.11 h to discharge (Kum et al.); 179 against 201 min stay, p = 0.33 (Wagner et al.); admissions 8 against 1 (Yusuf et al.); pain before and after not significantly changed (Lee and Coralic).

evidence.locator: Results, Studies on topical capsaicin (p. 498, right column); Table 3, Dean et al. row (p. 500)
evidence.extracted: Randomized trial of capsaicin against placebo cream (Dean et al.): no significant difference in self-reported nausea at 30 min (difference -2.0 cm, interval printed 0.2 to -4.2 cm); complete resolution of nausea 29.4% against 0% (risk ratio printed 3.4); mean nausea lower at 60 min; no differences in disposition or need for rescue antiemetics; exclusion criteria changed midway through recruitment.

evidence.locator: Table 2, Kum et al., Lee and Coralic, Wagner et al. and Yusuf et al. rows (pp. 496-499); Results, Studies on topical capsaicin (pp. 498-499)
evidence.extracted: Kum et al. (n = 201): 55% against 21% reached the efficacy outcome (p<0.001), time to discharge 3.72 against 6.11 h (p = 0.001), with the capsaicin group having received more drugs beforehand. Lee and Coralic (n = 57): no significant change in pain scores before and after, no adverse drug events. Wagner et al. (n = 43): length of stay 179 against 201 min (p = 0.33), fewer additional medicines. Yusuf et al. (n = 56): no differences in stay, medicines or 72-hour returns; 8 admissions with capsaicin against 1 without.

evidence.locator: Results, paragraph after Table 2 (p. 498, left column); Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 501); Limitations (p. 502)
evidence.extracted: Both randomized trials were judged at high risk of bias (loss to follow-up) and the retrospective studies mostly moderate to high; the authors find mixed evidence for capsaicin, note it is not known to have serious side effects though application may be uncomfortable, and call for rigorous trials.

risk_of_bias.note: The only trial is at high risk of bias (loss to follow-up, criteria changed during recruitment); the other studies are retrospective, moderate to high risk; seen second-hand through a review rated critically low.

inconsistency.note: Results split between benefit and no difference, one with more admissions.

indirectness.note: Emergency department patients with cannabis hyperemesis syndrome, as worded.

imprecision.note: About 30 randomized patients; no pooled estimate.

grade.reasoning: Starting from the one randomized trial (high), risk of bias -2, inconsistency -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. Status mixed: the studies disagree without an established reason. Insufficient evidence: neither benefit nor its absence is shown. Hot showers, often reported by patients as giving relief, and stopping cannabis were outside this review and remain untested here.
